Miasma Phantom Gyp: python.exe (gyp parser) spawning node index.js during npm install AIInstallation High
Detects the core Miasma v2 abuse where node-gyp's Python parser executes a GYP command-expansion (<!(...)>) embedded in binding.gyp, spawning the credential-stealer payload as a child of python.exe rather than via package.json lifecycle hooks. Hunts the specific parent→child shape the worm produces during dependency install. Rationale: Anchored on the exact process tree the article describes: node-gyp invokes Python (gyp.py) to parse binding.gyp, and the embedded <!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c) command spawns node.exe with index.js as a direct child of python.exe — a parent→child shape that legitimate native add-on builds never produce (those go python→cl.exe/link.exe/cmake.exe). Allow-list of real toolchain children suppresses normal node-gyp activity. Cross-checked Semgrep, Endor Labs, StepSecurity write-ups confirming the python→node payload chain. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://corgea.com/research/miasma-phantom-gyp-npm-worm-vapi-ai-sdk-ollama-june-2026
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate packages (e.g. node-pre-gyp, node-sass forks) where binding.gyp uses <!(node -e '...') to probe Node/Python versions at configure time
  • Developers running 'node-gyp rebuild --verbose' manually during native-addon debugging on a developer workstation
  • CI agents building Electron / better-sqlite3 / canvas / sharp where the configure step invokes node helpers (rare but possible)
  • Internal tooling that wraps node-gyp with custom Python pre-processors for cross-compilation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","--target_platform","--target_arch") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e" and ProcessCommandLine has "process.version")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full process tree (npm.cmd → node.exe → python.exe → matching child). Inspect the binding.gyp at the parent's working directory (look for <!(...), <!@(...), or pymod_do_main tokens); review the child's command line for 'index.js' or sandbox-escape Python literals. Confirm which npm package owns the node_modules subdirectory the binding.gyp came from. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from network, revoke any npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault tokens that resided on it (Miasma harvests all of these), force-rotate the developer's npm 2FA recovery codes, and pause CI runners using the same npm cache. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountObjectId across DeviceFileEvents for reads of ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml in the same window; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to api.github.com / *.workers.dev from that node.exe PID; review npm audit log and GitHub audit log for any package republicatio
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","node-gyp","binding.gyp","gyp_main")
| where FileName !in~ ("cl.exe","link.exe","cmake.exe","msbuild.exe","gcc.exe","g++.exe","clang.exe","clang++.exe","make.exe","nmake.exe","ld.exe","tracker.exe","rc.exe","cvtres.exe","mt.exe","conhost.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node","cmd.exe","sh","bash","dash","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("index.js","__subclasses__","catch_warnings","echo stub.c","/dev/null 2>&1","__import__('os')","pymod_do_main")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("node_modules","npm-cache","_npx","yarn","pnpm") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]python3?(\.exe)?$"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","node-gyp","binding.gyp","gyp_main")
| where not(ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](cl|link|cmake|msbuild|gcc|g\+\+|clang|clang\+\+|make|nmake|ld|tracker|rc|cvtres|mt|conhost)\.exe$")
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](node|cmd|sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("index.js","__subclasses__","catch_warnings","echo stub.c","/dev/null 2>&1","__import__('os')","pymod_do_main")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

title: Miasma Phantom Gyp - Python gyp parser spawning Node payload via binding.gyp
id: 7f3b6c2a-d4e1-4a01-9c5e-3a4f1c8e7b22
description: Detects node-gyp's Python parser (gyp.py) spawning unexpected child processes during npm install, indicative of GYP command-expansion abuse used by the Miasma v2 / Phantom Gyp worm (June 2026)
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/exploring-binding-gyp-npm-build-system
  - https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
  - https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_python_gyp:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'gyp.py'
      - 'node-gyp'
      - 'binding.gyp'
  suspicious_child_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\sh.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  suspicious_child_cmdline:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'index.js'
      - '__subclasses__'
      - 'catch_warnings'
      - 'echo stub.c'
      - "__import__('os')"
      - 'pymod_do_main'
  filter_compilers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cl.exe'
      - '\link.exe'
      - '\cmake.exe'
      - '\msbuild.exe'
      - '\gcc.exe'
      - '\clang.exe'
      - '\make.exe'
      - '\nmake.exe'
  condition: parent_python_gyp and (suspicious_child_image or suspicious_child_cmdline) and not filter_compilers
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate packages whose binding.gyp uses <!(node ...) for non-malicious build-time configuration (e.g. node-pre-gyp version probing)
  - Developers manually invoking node-gyp rebuild for native add-on debugging
level: high

Miasma-tainted package install: binding.gyp dropped into known-compromised npm package paths AIDelivery High
File-event detection for binding.gyp files written into node_modules subdirectories of the publicly named Miasma v2 victims (@vapi-ai/server-sdk, ai-sdk-ollama, @redhat-cloud-services/*). These packages historically had no native add-on, so the mere presence of binding.gyp inside their node_modules path is the campaign signature. Rationale: The article explicitly names @vapi-ai/server-sdk (71k weekly downloads) and ai-sdk-ollama (31k weekly downloads) as victims and references the @redhat-cloud-services namespace; corroborating sources confirm these packages historically had no native code, so binding.gyp inside their tree is the campaign signature. Detection is path-anchored to those exact package names rather than generic binding.gyp activity. Cross-checked Semgrep, Chainguard, and Endor Labs. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/chainguard-artifacts-safe-from-miasma-phantom-gyp-npm-attack • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1505.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vendor-published clean (post-incident) version of one of these packages ships a legitimate binding.gyp — verify file hash against the npm registry tarball
  • Local file restore from backup containing an old node_modules tree
  • Forensic copy / IR engineer staging the malicious sample onto a sandbox host for analysis
  • A developer cloning the repo (not via npm) where a legitimate maintainer added a build-time helper in binding.gyp
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the dropped binding.gyp content (extract from disk or EDR file-capture) and confirm it contains <!(...), <!@(...), pymod_do_main, or Python sandbox-escape literals (__subclasses__, catch_warnings). Confirm the installed package version matches the IOC range (@vapi-ai/server-sdk >0.11.0, ai-sdk-ollama >0.13.0). Step 2 — Contain: stop any in-flight node-gyp rebuild PID, isolate the host, and treat ALL credentials reachable from the host as burned — npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI configs, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, .npmrc auth. Trigger automated rotation. Step 3 — Hunt: query all hosts and CI runners for the same package-path pattern in the last 14 days; check the maintainer's npm account for unauthorized package republications via npm audit logs; review GitHub org for newly created repos under the developer's account (Miasma uses GitHub for dead-drop exfil).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any (
    @"node_modules\@vapi-ai\server-sdk",
    "node_modules/@vapi-ai/server-sdk",
    @"node_modules\ai-sdk-ollama",
    "node_modules/ai-sdk-ollama",
    @"node_modules\@redhat-cloud-services",
    "node_modules/@redhat-cloud-services")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    @"node_modules\@vapi-ai\server-sdk",
    "node_modules/@vapi-ai/server-sdk",
    @"node_modules\ai-sdk-ollama",
    "node_modules/ai-sdk-ollama",
    @"node_modules\@redhat-cloud-services",
    "node_modules/@redhat-cloud-services")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Miasma payload SHA256 hash hit (published Phantom Gyp IOCs) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based match for the four SHA256s associated with the Miasma v2 Phantom Gyp payload set. Fires on either file write or process execution telemetry. Universal IOC sweep across endpoint estate. Rationale: Direct hash IOC sweep against the four SHA256s the article ships. Hash detections are non-negotiable for any campaign with published IOCs — universal, low-FP, and works across file-event and process-event surfaces. Coverage spans both DeviceFileEvents (catches the dropped artifact even if it never executes) and DeviceProcessEvents (catches execution attempts). Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst or malware researcher intentionally placing the IOC sample on a sandbox / detonation host
  • Security tooling (e.g. EDR test harness, YARA-rule unit test fixtures) staging the hash for validation
  • Threat-intel platform pre-caching the file for hash-lookup tests
  • Inbound email or chat attachment carrying the sample for IR analysis (will hit Defender mail scan first)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("SOC-SANDBOX-01","IR-WORKSTATION-01","MALWARE-LAB-01")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned forensic / sandbox / IR-analyst workstation by checking the device tag and the user's role in IdentityInfo. Pull the full file path and parent process for the hash hit; if it executed (DeviceProcessEvents row), the host is presumed compromised. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device immediately via Live Response / Defender machine action, suspend the user's npm / GitHub / cloud sessions, kill the offending PID. Treat all secrets reachable from the host as burned and force rotation (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, .npmrc auth, kubeconfig, Vault tokens). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountObjectId and SHA256 across the full estate for the last 30 days; check whether any package on npm under the user's maintainer account was published in the same window (Miasma republishes from victim hosts); review GitHub audit log for new repos under the user's account in the last 7 days (potential dead-drop exfil endpoint).

Node child of node-gyp/python making outbound to GitHub dead-drop or anomalous web service during install AIexfil Medium
Catches the Miasma exfiltration step: after the binding.gyp command-expansion fires, the spawned node.exe (running index.js) beacons cloud credentials and CI tokens out to attacker-controlled GitHub repositories or webhook services. Pivots on the rare combination of node.exe with a node-gyp/python ancestor making outbound TCP to api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, or first-seen external hosts. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described post-execution behavior (credential exfil to attacker-controlled dead-drops) with the parent-process chain unique to binding.gyp abuse. Corroborating sources (Endor Labs, Morphisec, OX Security) confirm Miasma exfils to GitHub dead-drop repos and uses Workers/webhook bouncers; this detection requires both the gyp ancestry AND the suspicious destination to fire, keeping FPs manageable while catching the campaign-specific exfil shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/its-in-your-ai-assistant-now-shai-hulud-wave-3-and-the-miasma-worm-targeting-npm/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/600000-monthly-downloads-affected-miasma-supply-chain-attack-is-back-on-npm/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm packages whose postinstall hook fetches assets from raw.githubusercontent.com (e.g. node-pre-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries) — but those typically run as direct child of npm, not via python.exe (gyp) chain
  • node-gyp packages that pull source tarballs from GitHub during configure step (rare; node-pre-gyp uses HTTP downloader)
  • CI runners that genuinely push to api.github.com via node-based GitHub API client called from a build hook
  • Cloudflare Workers used by an org's internal build accelerator service
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install") and DstHostname has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the spawning binding.gyp content and the node process's full argv; identify which npm package owns the source path. Check whether the GitHub destination repo is org-controlled (legitimate) or an externally owned account (likely dead-drop). Step 2 — Contain: kill the node.exe PID, isolate the device, and immediately rotate every credential reachable from the host — focus first on the developer's GitHub PAT (worm publishes via it), npm publish token, AWS keys in ~/.aws/credentials, .npmrc auth, kubeconfig, Vault tokens, GCP/Azure CLI cache. Step 3 — Hunt: query GitHub audit log for new repository creations under the developer's user account in the last 24h (Miasma creates ephemeral dead-drop repos); search ImNetworkSession for any other node.exe egress to the same destination from CI runners in the last 7 days; check npm registry for unauthorized package publications under the dev's maintainer accounts.
let gyp_node_children = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "node.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","cmd.exe","sh","bash")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","binding.gyp","node-gyp")
        or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe")
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project ProcSpawnTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com",".workers.dev","webhook.site","ngrok.io","hooks.slack.com","discord.com/api/webhooks","transfer.sh","file.io","0x0.st")
   or RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner gyp_node_children on DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.ProcessId
| where Timestamp between (ProcSpawnTime .. ProcSpawnTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GypParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine1
| order by Timestamp desc
let gyp_node_children = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]node(\.exe)?$"
    | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](python3?|cmd|sh|bash)(\.exe)?$"
    | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","binding.gyp","node-gyp")
    | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
    | project ProcSpawnTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ParentProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com",".workers.dev","webhook.site","ngrok.io","hooks.slack.com","discord.com","transfer.sh","file.io","0x0.st")
| join kind=inner gyp_node_children on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ProcSpawnTime .. ProcSpawnTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, ParentProcessCommandLine
source:(windows.sysmon OR crowdstrike) @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) (@DestinationHostname:(*api.github.com* OR *raw.githubusercontent.com* OR *.workers.dev OR *webhook.site* OR *ngrok.io* OR *hooks.slack.com* OR *discord.com* OR *transfer.sh* OR *file.io* OR *0x0.st*))

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Wait, binding.gyp Can Do What? Exploring npm's Weirdest Build System
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("index.js", "node.js", "evil.js", "evil_script.js", "malicious.js", "evil.sh", "cc-evil.sh", "evil-wrapper.sh", "cc-evil-wrapper.sh"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents

WinRAR Flaw Exploited by Russia-Aligned Groups to Deploy Stealers in Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 16 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Two Russia-aligned cyber attack campaigns have continued to exploit a security flaw in WinRAR to target Ukrainian organisations, almost a year after patches for the vulnerability were released. The activity has been attributed by Trend Micro to Earth Dahu (aka Gamaredon) and SHADOW-EARTH-066 (aka UAC-0226). It involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw that allows an

Exploitation. Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GIFTEDCROOK browser credential and cookie theft — non-browser process reads Chromium/Firefox stores · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 — archive tool writes payload to user Startup folder AIInstallation High
Detects the smoking-gun signature of CVE-2025-8088 NTFS ADS path traversal: WinRAR/Rar/UnRAR/7zG writing files into %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup — the exact persistence drop chain used by SHADOW-EARTH-066 (GIFTEDCROOK) and Earth Dahu (GammaPhish/GammaLoad) campaigns against Ukrainian organisations. Rationale: Article explicitly states the CVE-2025-8088 exploit chain drops an LNK 'placed in the Startup folder so that it's automatically executed every time a user logs in' — combining archive-tool parent with Startup-folder destination + autostart extension is article-specific and behaviourally near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against Trend Micro disclosure and ESET's earlier RomCom write-up of the same CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-8088 • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/romcom-exploits-winrar-zero-day-cve-2025-8088/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0047/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1574.005 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT-deployed software bundles where WinRAR/7-Zip is used in scripted installers that legitimately drop launcher shortcuts into the Startup folder
  • User extracts a legitimate portable app archive and manually pins an LNK into Startup (rare but seen on dev/power-user workstations)
  • Backup-restore operations where an old user profile is recovered with Startup-folder content via WinRAR
  • Software-deployment tools (PDQ Deploy, SCCM staging) chain-calling WinRAR/UnRAR to expand a vendor MSI bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PDQDeploy","sccm","sccmclient","InstallShield","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the dropped artefact (LNK/EXE/DLL), SHA256 it, and check VT + the article's known-bad hashes; inspect the parent RAR file in DownloadedFiles / mail attachments. 2) Contain — isolate the host via MDE Live Response, kill any running powershell/cmd/mshta children spawned in the next 5 minutes, and quarantine the dropped Startup artefact. 3) Hunt — sweep the org for the parent RAR hash, any sibling NTFS:$DATA ADS writes by the same WinRAR process tree, and pivot on the user mailbox for the inbound phishing message that delivered the archive (last 14 days).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("WinRAR.exe","Rar.exe","UnRAR.exe","7zG.exe","Bandizip.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".ps1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zg.exe","bandizip.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("lnk","exe","dll","bat","vbs","hta","cmd","ps1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS Path Traversal — Archive Tool Writes to Startup Folder
id: 9b3f8e2a-1f5d-4c1a-9b3e-5e7f8c2d4a1b
description: Detects archive extraction utilities writing autostart payloads to the user Startup folder, the smoking-gun signature of CVE-2025-8088 NTFS ADS path traversal abuse used by SHADOW-EARTH-066 and Earth Dahu against Ukrainian targets.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/winrar-flaw-exploited-by-russia-aligned.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  archive_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\WinRAR.exe'
      - '\Rar.exe'
      - '\UnRAR.exe'
      - '\7zG.exe'
      - '\Bandizip.exe'
  startup_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
  autostart_ext:

      - '.lnk'
      - '.exe'
      - '.dll'
      - '.bat'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.hta'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.ps1'
  condition: archive_tool and startup_path and autostart_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\WinRAR.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\Rar.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\UnRAR.exe OR *\unrar.exe OR *\7zG.exe OR *\Bandizip.exe) @TargetFilename:(*"\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\"* OR *"\\start menu\\programs\\startup\\"*)

| TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\.*\.(lnk|exe|dll|bat|vbs|hta|cmd|ps1)$/i

Startup LNK spawns cmd.exe → PowerShell in-memory DLL loader (GIFTEDCROOK chain) AIInstallation High
Catches the GIFTEDCROOK post-extraction loader chain: explorer.exe auto-runs a Startup LNK that invokes cmd.exe which spawns powershell.exe carrying in-memory reflective-load primitives to launch result.dll. Article calls out cmd→PowerShell→reflective-load as the exact sequence. Rationale: Article describes the chain verbatim: 'LNK in Startup folder ... spawns a PowerShell loader via cmd.exe, which then uses in-memory DLL loading to ultimately launch ... result.dll.' Triple-anchor (Startup-LNK parent + cmd→PS + reflective-load tokens) is highly article-specific and rare in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/ • https://www.cert.gov.ua/article/giftedcrook
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1620 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin login script that uses cmd.exe → powershell.exe -EncodedCommand from an admin's pinned Startup shortcut
  • Citrix/RDS broker scripts triggered from per-user logon LNKs (some EHRs/VDI gold images still ship these)
  • Vendor monitoring/inventory tools that use cmd→PS reflective load (LANDesk, older Tanium build-out scripts)
  • Developer-machine PowerShell profile that imports modules via Reflection.Assembly from a Startup shim
Suppression filter
| where not (ActorUsername has_any ("admin","svc-") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Import-Module","-File \\\\","\\Scripts\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the powershell.exe command line + decode any base64; if it references result.dll or in-memory load, treat as confirmed GIFTEDCROOK loader and pull the Startup LNK + its $DATA streams. 2) Contain — isolate host, kill the powershell.exe tree, quarantine the LNK target and any DLLs written by the PS session in the prior 60 seconds. 3) Hunt — query DeviceNetworkEvents from the powershell.exe ProcessId for callbacks to the article's IPs/domains; sweep all hosts for the same LNK target hash and same parent RAR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", ".lnk")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("FromBase64String","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Reflection.Assembly","[Reflection.Assembly]","::Load(","-nop","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-enc","result.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "cmd.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", ".lnk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FromBase64String","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Reflection.Assembly","::Load(","-nop","hidden","-enc","result.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*"\\Startup\\"* OR *"\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup"* OR *.lnk*) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*FromBase64String* OR *Reflection.Assembly* OR *::Load(* OR *IEX* OR *Invoke-Expression* OR *-nop* OR *hidden* OR *-enc* OR *result.dll*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/cmd\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| ParentCommandLine=/(\\Startup\\|\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup|\.lnk)/i
| regex("(FromBase64String|Reflection\\.Assembly|::Load\\(|IEX|Invoke-Expression|-nop|hidden|-enc|result\\.dll)", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="cmd.exe" AND (Processes.parent_process="*\\Startup\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*Reflection.Assembly*" OR Processes.process="*::Load(*" OR Processes.process="*IEX*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*" OR Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="cmd.exe" AND (Processes.parent_process="*\\Startup\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*Reflection.Assembly*" OR Processes.process="*::Load(*" OR Processes.process="*IEX*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*" OR Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
GIFTEDCROOK browser credential and cookie theft — non-browser process reads Chromium/Firefox stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects GIFTEDCROOK's credential-collection stage: a process that is NOT the browser itself opens the Login Data, Cookies, Web Data or Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite files inside the user's browser profile directories. Article names Chrome, Edge, Opera and Firefox as the targets. Rationale: Article enumerates exact targets: 'passwords and cookies from Chromium-based browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Opera) and Mozilla Firefox.' File-access pattern from non-browser process is the highest-signal credential-theft pivot available without YARA. Matches GIFTEDCROOK behavior in Trend Micro and CERT-UA reports. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/giftedcrook • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Credential-manager browser plugins backed by a helper EXE (1Password Helper, Bitwarden-cli)
  • Endpoint backup agents (Code42/CrashPlan, Druva) that snapshot the entire user profile including the browser data directory
  • DLP agents (Forcepoint, Netskope) that scan profile contents on first sync
  • User-account migration tools (USMT, Microsoft Edge Profile Importer, Chrome migration helper) during machine provisioning
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("1Password.exe","1PasswordHelper.exe","Bitwarden.exe","keeperpasswordmanager.exe","code42service.exe","crashplanservice.exe","druvainsync.exe","nsdiag.exe","fcdblog.exe","USMT.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the reading process is not on the allow-list; SHA256 the binary, check parent process tree back to explorer.exe/cmd.exe/PowerShell to determine entry vector. 2) Contain — isolate host, force-reset all stored credentials and active SSO sessions for the affected user (Entra revoke + browser-side sign-out), rotate any saved API keys, kill the offending process. 3) Hunt — pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet; check DeviceNetworkEvents from the same ProcessId for exfil to article IOCs; review EmailEvents for the inbound RAR.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","opera.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","opera.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GIFTEDCROOK / Gamaredon C2 callback to article IOCs (IPs + workers.dev / trycloudflare / .ru domains) AICommand & Control Medium
Network-level pivot on the article's published infrastructure: three IPs and seven domains spanning Cloudflare Workers, trycloudflare quick tunnels and Russia-tied vanity domains used by SHADOW-EARTH-066 and Earth Dahu after pivoting away from Telegram as their exfil channel. Rationale: All ten IOCs are taken directly from the article's provided IOC bundle (3 IPs, 7 domains) and triangulate two distinct campaigns sharing the CVE. The workers.dev + trycloudflare-quick-tunnel + .ru-vanity-domain combination is the article-specific tradecraft signature post-Telegram-blocking pivot. Triple-pivot (DNS, network, proxy) maximises catch rate. Cross-checked against: • https://otx.alienvault.com/indicator/domain/dayobtvoyu.ru • https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/172.86.76.132 • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate dev/test traffic to other tenants on the workers.dev or trycloudflare.com shared CDN — possible but the specific subdomains are unique
  • Sandbox/research VM in the same network deliberately detonating GIFTEDCROOK samples
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment agent that performs active checks against the same IOCs
  • Security researcher browsing the article and clicking links to defanged-but-still-resolvable IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("CuckooMon.exe","vmtoolsd.exe","sandbox-agent.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX-","DETONATE-","MALLAB-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that made the call; if it's powershell/wscript/mshta/cmd/rundll32, treat as confirmed C2. 2) Contain — block the IPs at the firewall/secure-web-gateway, sinkhole the domains in internal DNS, isolate any host that connected in the last 30 days. 3) Hunt — for every host that touched any IOC pull the parent RAR file, LNK Startup artefact, and any FileWritten events under the user's AppData in the 24h before contact; check EmailEvents for the inbound message that delivered the archive.
let bad_domains = dynamic(["snterval.selltosell.ru","dayobtvoyu.ru","sweet.csxvl00328.workers.dev","csxvl00328.workers.dev","e097.yggjf81487.workers.dev","vids-road-christina-guards.trycloudflare.com","insight-sweet-drainage-appreciated.trycloudflare.com"]);
let bad_ips = dynamic(["172.86.76.132","144.172.88.24","172.86.72.243"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (bad_domains) or RemoteIP in (bad_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let bad_domains = dynamic(["snterval.selltosell.ru","dayobtvoyu.ru","sweet.csxvl00328.workers.dev","csxvl00328.workers.dev","e097.yggjf81487.workers.dev","vids-road-christina-guards.trycloudflare.com","insight-sweet-drainage-appreciated.trycloudflare.com"]);
let bad_ips = dynamic(["172.86.76.132","144.172.88.24","172.86.72.243"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any (bad_domains) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, IndicatorType="DNS"),
    (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (bad_ips) or DstHostname has_any (bad_domains) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, IndicatorType="Network"),
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (bad_ips) or RequestURL has_any (bad_domains) or DestinationHostName has_any (bad_domains) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=DeviceName, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP, DstHostname=DestinationHostName, URL=RequestURL, IndicatorType="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Earth Dahu / Gamaredon HTA-to-VBScript chain (mshta.exe spawning wscript/cscript) AIDelivery High
Detects Earth Dahu's documented HTA-to-VBScript delivery chain: mshta.exe loading GammaPhish HTA, then spawning wscript.exe/cscript.exe to execute GammaLoad VBScript downloaders that pull GammaSteel. Article confirms this chain has been active since September 2025 and through at least April 2026. Rationale: Article quotes Trend Micro: 'Earth Dahu used the vulnerability with an HTA-to-VBScript infection chain that delivered espionage modules' — mshta.exe → wscript.exe parent-child with a remote/.hta argument is the canonical GammaPhish→GammaLoad pivot. Cross-checked with Sekoia's recent Gamaredon write-up and MITRE G0047. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0047/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.005 T1105 T1568.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business application that ships .hta installers (rare but seen in healthcare and Ukrainian government estates)
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic .hta scripts from Microsoft KB downloads
  • Vendor support tools (Dell SupportAssist older builds, some HP printer setup utilities) launched via mshta.exe
  • Internal IT job that wraps a vbscript downloader for software inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("HELPDESK-","SCCM-") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\corp.local\\","\\\\fileserver\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — extract the .hta URL/path from ParentCommandLine, fetch it in a sandbox, hash the dropped VBScript and compare against the article's published hashes (GammaLoad/GammaSteel families). 2) Contain — isolate the host, kill the mshta/wscript tree, block the .hta URL at the proxy, sinkhole any Dead-Drop-Resolver-style domain returned in the GammaLoad fetch chain. 3) Hunt — sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound calls from wscript/cscript to non-Microsoft hosts in the last 30 days; pull EmailEvents and DeviceFileEvents from WinRAR for the inbound RAR that triggered the chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta","http://","https://","javascript:","vbscript:")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".js",".jse","GetObject(","WScript.Shell","MSXML2.XMLHTTP","WinHttp.WinHttpRequest")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta","http://","https://","javascript:","vbscript:")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".js",".jse","GetObject(","WScript.Shell","MSXML2.XMLHTTP","WinHttp.WinHttpRequest")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Earth Dahu (Gamaredon) HTA-to-VBScript Infection Chain via mshta.exe
id: 4f8e2c1d-7a9b-4d3e-8c5f-2e7a9b1c4d8f
description: Detects the GammaPhish HTA → GammaLoad VBScript chain — mshta.exe loading a remote .hta and spawning wscript/cscript or PowerShell, as documented by Trend Micro and Sekoia for the Earth Dahu / Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/winrar-flaw-exploited-by-russia-aligned.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.t1218.005
  - attack.t1059.005
  - attack.execution
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_mshta:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\mshta.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - '.hta'
      - 'http://'
      - 'https://'
      - 'javascript:'
      - 'vbscript:'
  child_scripthost:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  condition: parent_mshta and child_scripthost
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\mshta.exe OR *\MSHTA.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*.hta* OR *http\://* OR *https\://* OR *javascript\:* OR *vbscript\:*) @Image:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\cmd.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/mshta\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|powershell|pwsh|cmd)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\.hta|https?://|javascript:|vbscript:)", field=ParentCommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentCommandLine, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="mshta.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(parent_process,"(?i)\.(hta|html?)|https?://|javascript:|vbscript:")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="mshta.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(parent_process,"(?i)\.(hta|html?)|https?://|javascript:|vbscript:")
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-09 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

University of Toronto researchers have built and tested a proof-of-concept AI-driven computer worm that uses a locally hosted open-weight large language model to reason its way through a network, generate tailored attack strategies for each target it encounters, and replicate itself, all without human intervention and without touching a commercial AI service. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
