title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

New FROST Attack Lets Websites Track What Sites and Apps You Open via SSD Timing

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 7 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious website can work out which sites you visit and which apps you open, using nothing but JavaScript and the timing of your SSD. The attack, called FROST, needs no native code, no extension, and no permission prompt. You open the page, leave the tab sitting there, and it watches the drive for contention in the background. Researchers at Graz University of Technology built it and

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Browser writing oversized OPFS file (potential FROST SSD-timing side-channel) AIReconnaissance Low
Hunts for a browser process (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari) writing a file >4 GB into the per-origin Origin Private File System storage path. FROST requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so reads bypass the page cache and reach the SSD — legitimate OPFS use rarely exceeds a few hundred MB, so an unexplained multi-GB OPFS allocation is the only host-side tell the Graz paper offers. Rationale: Anchored on the only host-side artefact the article actually names: 'watching your browser's storage for an unexplained multi-gigabyte file is another tell.' The >4 GB threshold mirrors FROST's stated requirement (file > physical RAM to defeat the page cache). Browser-process scope + per-origin OPFS path roots (Chrome/Edge: 'File System/' inside the profile; Firefox: 'storage/default/...fs/'; Safari/WebKit: 'Library/Safari/Storage' or 'Library/WebKit') are taken from the standardised OPFS-on-disk locations referenced by the W3C spec the article cites. No external corroboration searched — there is no actor / malware family / CVE attached, and the IOCs extracted by the pipeline (malicious.app, victim.com, receiver.app, sender.app) are clearly academic placeholders from the paper, not real C2.
ATT&CKT1592.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-browser IDEs (StackBlitz WebContainers, VS Code for the Web, Replit, GitPod) which legitimately allocate multi-GB OPFS sandboxes for projects
  • Web-based media editors (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web) caching large source files
  • Browser-based games persisting asset bundles or save state to OPFS
  • Profile sync / migration tooling temporarily staging the user's browser profile inside the same directory tree
  • Service-worker caches for offline-first PWAs (e.g. mapping apps) that legitimately swell over time
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stackblitz", "webcontainer", "vscode-web", "replit", "gitpod", "photopea", "figma", "capcut"))
// Add per-tenant: exclude origin folders for sanctioned in-browser IDEs / editors after one pass of investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the origin that owns the OPFS slice (the path component immediately under '/File System/' or '/storage/default/' is the URL-encoded origin). Check the user's recent browser history / open tabs for that origin and whether it is a known-good web IDE / media editor. Pull the parent browser commandline to confirm it's an interactive session and not a headless automation harness. Step 2 — Contain: if the origin is unknown / suspicious, ask the user to close the tab (article notes the measurement only runs while the tab is open) and clear site-data for that origin in browser settings. Snapshot the OPFS file before deletion for forensic review. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same origin across the fleet — if multiple users have a >4 GB OPFS slice from the same domain, that domain is the indicator, not the file size. Also review whether the same browser session enabled cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) by checking proxy/Zscaler/CSP-report telemetry, since FROST 
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\File System\", "/File System/", "/storage/default/", ".mozilla/firefox", "/Library/Safari/Storage", "/Library/WebKit")
| where FileSize > 4000000000  // 4 GB — FROST requires file > physical RAM
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome","msedge","firefox","brave","Safari","WebKit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\File System\", "/File System/", "/storage/default/", ".mozilla/firefox", "/Library/Safari/Storage", "/Library/WebKit")
| where TargetFileSize > 4000000000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize
| order by TargetFileSize desc
title: Browser writes oversized Origin Private File System (OPFS) file - possible FROST SSD timing side-channel
id: 3f1e9a2c-1d6e-4f0a-9c4f-2b9b5e6a7c01
status: experimental
description: Detects a browser process allocating an unusually large file (>4 GB) inside its per-origin OPFS storage directory. The FROST attack (Graz Univ. of Technology, DIMVA 2026) requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so SSD-timing reads bypass the page cache.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-frost-attack-lets-websites-track.html
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.t1592.004
  - attack.reconnaissance
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '/Google Chrome'
      - '/firefox'
      - '/Safari'
      - '/com.apple.WebKit.Networking'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\File System\'
      - '/File System/'
      - '/storage/default/'
      - '.mozilla/firefox'
      - '/Library/Safari/Storage'
      - '/Library/WebKit'
  selection_size:
    FileSize|gte: 4000000000
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - In-browser IDEs (StackBlitz WebContainers, VS Code Web, Replit, GitPod local) genuinely use multi-GB OPFS
  - Web-based video / photo editors caching large media (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web)
  - Browser-based game engines persisting save state / asset bundles
level: low
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe) OR @process.name:(chrome OR firefox OR Safari OR Google\ Chrome)) (@TargetFilename:(*\File\ System\* OR */File\ System/* OR */storage/default/* OR *.mozilla/firefox/* OR */Library/Safari/Storage/* OR */Library/WebKit/*)) @file.size:>4000000000
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|Safari|WebKit)/i
| regex("(File System|storage/default|\\.mozilla/firefox|Library/Safari/Storage|Library/WebKit)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[sum(WrittenBytes, as=BytesWritten), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])
| BytesWritten > 4000000000
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, max(Filesystem.file_size) as max_size from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\File System\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/File System/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/storage/default/*/fs/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla/firefox/*/storage/default/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/Safari/Storage/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/WebKit/*/Storage/*") AND Filesystem.file_size>4000000000 by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, max(Filesystem.file_size) as max_size from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\File System\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/File System/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/storage/default/*/fs/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla/firefox/*/storage/default/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/Safari/Storage/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/WebKit/*/Storage/*") AND Filesystem.file_size>4000000000 by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Installation. Hades/Miasma PyPI poisoned package installation (26 named packages) AIDelivery High
Detects pip / python invoking installation of any of the 26 PyPI packages and versions Socket / StepSecurity identified in the Hades wave of the Miasma supply-chain campaign. Catches the very first foothold before the *-setup.pth hook runs on next interpreter start. Rationale: Uses the verbatim 26 package names from the article's two Hades clusters (the 19-package PyPI cluster + the 7-package bioinformatics cluster). Pip-install command line with these exact names is effectively zero-FP outside of incident-response activity.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR / threat-intel analyst intentionally pulling the package into a sandbox for reverse engineering
  • Internal package-mirror sync (e.g. Artifactory / Nexus PyPI proxy) caching the malicious release before takedown
  • Bioinformatics researcher pulling a legitimately-named-but-coincidental fork via an internal index URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "sandbox" and FolderPath !has "\\malware_analysis\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot to DeviceFileEvents on the same host for any *-setup.pth file created after the install and any DeviceNetworkEvents to github.com/oven-sh/bun within 30 min — confirms full chain executed. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke all developer secrets present (GitHub PAT, npm/PyPI tokens, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, .ssh/*, Anthropic/Claude/MCP configs), force-rotate before reconnecting. 3) Hunt: search the org for any other host that pulled the same package versions in the last 14 days; check internal package mirrors for cached copies; check GitHub org for any repo with description matching 'Hades*The End for the Damned' indicating exfil happened.

Python interpreter downloading Bun runtime ZIP from oven-sh GitHub release AIInstallation High
Hades/Miasma stages a JavaScript stealer by having the malicious .pth or __init__.py hook download the standalone Bun runtime ZIP from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. Detecting Python/pip as the parent of that network connection is the cleanest cross-platform pivot — Bun is not a Python dependency in any normal supply chain. Rationale: Article: 'The compromised releases shipped a *-setup.pth file that attempts to execute automatically during Python startup, download the Bun JavaScript runtime, and run an obfuscated JavaScript payload named _index.js.' StepSecurity also notes Bun is downloaded as a standalone ZIP — pivoting on python→github.com/oven-sh/bun is the staging-link signature.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually running 'pip install bun-py' or any pip wrapper that legitimately fetches Bun for a project
  • CI job using a Python-based installer/bootstrap (e.g. Ansible play that installs Bun on a dev workstation)
  • Container build step where a Python entrypoint legitimately bootstraps a Bun-based JS toolchain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-py","install-bun","@nestjs","bunx"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python's command line — was the install one of the 26 Hades package names? Pull DeviceFileEvents for any .pth or _index.js write between the Python start and the Bun download. 2) Contain: kill the Bun process tree, isolate host, snapshot ~/.bun and any extracted ZIP for forensics, revoke every dev secret the user owns (GitHub PAT, npm token, PyPI token, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI creds, Anthropic/Claude API key). 3) Hunt: look across the org for any other host where python.exe was the parent of a github.com/oven-sh/bun fetch in the last 30 days; check GitHub Actions audit log for the user's PAT scopes being used from unfamiliar runners.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com")
   and (RemoteUrl has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or RemoteUrl endswith ".zip")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
       or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
    | project DeviceId, PyTimestamp = Timestamp, PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine
) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (PyTimestamp .. PyTimestamp + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, PyCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunUrlFrag = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (BunUrlFrag)
| where Url has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or Url endswith ".zip"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","pip")
    | project DvcHostname, PyTime = TimeGenerated, PyCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (PyTime .. PyTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, PyCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades persistence: *-setup.pth file written into Python site-packages AIInstallation High
The Hades cluster persists by dropping a `*-setup.pth` file into a site-packages directory. Python's `site` module executes any `import`/`exec` line in a `.pth` file at every interpreter start, so this file is the auto-run primitive. Detect creation of any file matching the pattern by a non-pip writer or with executable content inside. Rationale: Article: 'the use of a *-setup.pth file that's processed by Python's site module during interpreter startup, resulting in the execution of the malicious payload after installation.' The `-setup.pth` suffix in site-packages is unusual — legitimate .pth files are typically named after the package (e.g. easy-install.pth, distutils-precedence.pth), not '<pkg>-setup.pth'.
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom internal setup.py / build backends that author a vendor-named '*-setup.pth' (rare but possible)
  • DFIR analyst restoring a sample for reversing into an isolated venv
  • Editable-install ('pip install -e') artefact named *-setup.pth from an unusual build tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--editable"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .pth contents (Defender 'Run query' / live response → small file, plain text). Genuine .pth files are single import lines; Hades .pth contains exec() / urllib code downloading Bun. 2) Contain: delete the .pth (it executes on every python start including services), isolate host, kill any running bun / _index.js processes, revoke developer secrets owned by AccountName. 3) Hunt: search every Python venv/system site-packages on the host and across the fleet for the same filename pattern; check whether the same SHA256 appears anywhere else; pivot to the parent pip install command and check whether it shows up on any other host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime reading developer credential files (.npmrc / .pypirc / .ssh / .env / cloud configs) AIActions on Objectives High
The Hades JavaScript stealer (_index.js) executes inside Bun and walks the developer's home directory for credentials: .npmrc, .pypirc, .env, .aws/credentials, .config/gcloud, .azure, .docker, ~/.ssh/, ~/.config/Claude, MCP configs, Vault tokens, shell histories. Bun touching those paths is the credential_access signature. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact target set: 'secrets associated with GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, CircleCI, Anthropic, AWS, GCP, Azure, and Kubernetes, along with Docker configurations, Vault tokens, SSH keys, shell histories, .env files, .npmrc files, .pypirc files, Claude/MCP configurations.' Bun as the reader is what makes this fire — legitimate dev tools (git, gh, aws-cli) reading these is normal; Bun reading 3+ distinct credential paths in one session is not.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bun-based dev tool (e.g. wrangler, supabase, drizzle) that legitimately reads .env for project config
  • Bun-based deployment script that reads .aws/credentials to deploy infra
  • Engineer running 'bun test' in a repo whose test setup reads ~/.npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wrangler","supabase","drizzle","vite","next","astro") and SecretReads < 5)
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every path Bun touched in the window (group by FolderPath); a 'real' Bun app reads ~/.env in its own project dir, malware fans out to .ssh, .aws AND .npmrc AND Claude AND .docker. Read the parent process — was Python the grandparent? Was a *-setup.pth file run? 2) Contain: kill all bun processes, isolate host, mass-revoke every secret in the read set (GitHub PATs, npm/PyPI tokens, AWS access keys, GCP service-account keys, Anthropic API keys, all SSH keys), force-rotate before reissue. 3) Hunt: pivot to GitHub audit log for unfamiliar PAT use; check the user's GitHub repos for new repos whose description matches 'Hades*The End for the Damned' (the campaign exfil marker); check whether the same Bun SHA256 has run on any other host.

gh-token-monitor service install or rm -rf wiper command (Hades self-destruct) AIActions on Objectives High
Hades installs a background service named 'gh-token-monitor' that doubles as a wiper — if the developer revokes the stolen GitHub token, the service triggers `rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`. Either the service-install or the wiper command is article-specific and warrants an alert. Rationale: Article: 'Install a background service named gh-token-monitor that acts as a wiper by removing all data (rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents) if the stolen GitHub token is revoked by the developer.' The service name and the exact wiper command line are both unique enough to alert directly on string match.
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1543.002 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team / purple-team replicating the Hades chain in a lab
  • Security researcher detonating the malware in a controlled VM with EDR shipping to prod tenant
  • Sysadmin's deliberate cleanup script that happens to chain rm -rf ~ with rm -rf ~/Documents (highly unusual)
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a CRITICAL — wiper attempts may already be running. Immediately check whether the rm -rf process completed and how much was destroyed (DeviceFileEvents on FileDeleted for the same DeviceId, last 5 min). 2) Contain: isolate host instantly (Defender Live Response 'isolate'), kill the gh-token-monitor service before it triggers, snapshot the disk for forensics, restore from backup if data is gone. 3) Hunt: search the whole fleet for the same service name and the same rm -rf command pattern in last 30 days; check GitHub audit log for the dev's PAT being used from unfamiliar runners (the wiper trigger is PAT revocation, so revocation may be in flight); search GitHub for any new repo by the user described 'Hades*The End for the Damned' indicating exfil completed before the wiper armed.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service","systemd")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | where AdditionalFields has "gh-token-monitor" or FileName has "gh-token-monitor" or ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event"
)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 7045
  | where ServiceName has "gh-token-monitor" or ServiceFileName has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event", ActingProcessCommandLine = ServiceFileName, DvcHostname = Computer, ActorUsername = SubjectUserName
)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Wiper Command or gh-token-monitor Service Install
id: 7c5b9e8a-2d3c-4f5b-9e7d-3a4b5c6d7e8a
description: Detects either installation of a service literally named 'gh-token-monitor' or execution of the Hades wiper command 'rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents' attributed to the Hades / Miasma PyPI campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1543.003
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_service:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'gh-token-monitor'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'sc create'
      - 'sc.exe create'
      - 'systemctl'
      - 'launchctl'
      - 'New-Service'
  selection_wiper:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'rm -rf'
      - 'Documents'
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|/home/|/Users/).*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents'
  condition: selection_service or selection_wiper
level: critical

(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:linux.auditd) AND ((@CommandLine:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @CommandLine:(*sc?create* OR *systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *New-Service*)) OR (@process.command_line:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @process.command_line:(*systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *sc?create*)) OR @CommandLine:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents") OR @process.command_line:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents"))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/gh-token-monitor/i AND CommandLine=/(sc\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|New-Service)/i) OR CommandLine=/rm\s+-rf\s+(~\/?|\/home\/[^\/\s]+|\/Users\/[^\/\s]+)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?\/?Documents/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
(`endpoint_processes` OR `linux_processes`)
| eval is_service_install=if(match(process,"(?i)gh-token-monitor") AND (match(process,"(?i)(sc\\.exe|sc\\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|new-service)")),1,0),
       is_wiper=if(match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+(~/?|/Users/[^/]+|/home/[^/]+)\\s*;\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~?/Documents") OR match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/?\\s*;?\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/Documents"),1,0)
| where is_service_install=1 OR is_wiper=1
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(process) as commands by host user parent_process_name process_name is_service_install is_wiper
Hades C2: GitHub commit search for campaign markers TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime / firedalazer AICommand & Control High
Hades retrieves staged payloads by polling the GitHub commits API for two unique marker strings: 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime' (Base64 JS payload) and 'firedalazer' (Python dropper). Either string appearing in process command lines, HTTP requests, or DNS/URL telemetry on a dev host is a high-fidelity C2 indicator. Rationale: Article: 'the malware queries GitHub commits for the keyword TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime to extract a Base64-encoded string containing a JavaScript payload. It also polls GitHub for commits matching the keyword firedalazer so as to fetch a Python-based dropper.' Both strings are sufficiently unique (random-looking concatenations) that any appearance in process/web/DNS telemetry is essentially zero-FP outside of threat-hunting activity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst pasting the IOC into a curl / gh CLI command for verification
  • Security tool (EDR, SOAR) running a containment query that includes the marker string
  • Internal blog/wiki page mentioning the IOC being fetched into a browser (unlikely on hash/URL telemetry, but possible in proxy logs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gh.exe","gh","curl.exe","curl") or AccountName !in~ ("soc-analyst","threat-intel")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which process/host issued the query — if it's a security analyst's gh CLI or a SOAR enrichment query, dismiss. If it's bun / python / a previously-unknown binary, treat as live C2. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the calling process tree, snapshot any retrieved payload from disk (look for base64 blobs / .py / .js dropped in the last hour), revoke every developer secret on the host. 3) Hunt: pivot fleet-wide for the same two strings in process and web telemetry over the last 60 days; check whether any host queried github.com/oven-sh/bun in the same window (would chain to UC 2); search GitHub commits for the same marker strings in the org's own repos.
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url
),
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "network", FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url = RemoteUrl
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "web", ActingProcessName = "", ActingProcessCommandLine = "", ActorUsername = SrcUsername
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Campaign GitHub C2 Marker Strings
id: 5a6b7c8d-9e0f-1a2b-3c4d-5e6f7a8b9c0d
description: Detects either of the two Hades / Miasma GitHub commit-marker strings (TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime, firedalazer) appearing in a process command line — the malware searches GitHub for these to retrieve Base64-encoded JS payload and the Python dropper respectively.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime'
      - 'firedalazer'
  condition: selection
level: high

(@CommandLine:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @process.command_line:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @DestinationHostname:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo ScriptContent=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, #event_simpleName], function=count())
NETWORK
(`endpoint_processes` Processes.process IN ("*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*","*firedalazer*"))
| eval pivot="process"
| append [ search `web_logs` (url="*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*" OR url="*firedalazer*" OR uri_query="*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*" OR uri_query="*firedalazer*") | eval pivot="web" ]
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(process) as commands values(url) as urls by host user pivot
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")

LiteLLM CVE-2026-42271 MCP test endpoint POST (preview command injection) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP POSTs to LiteLLM's vulnerable MCP test endpoints (/mcp-rest/test/connection and /mcp-rest/test/tools/list) that accept full stdio server configurations and spawn arbitrary commands as the proxy user. Both endpoints are pre-patch attacker entrypoints called out by BerriAI and Horizon3.ai. Rationale: Both URIs are named verbatim in BerriAI's advisory and the article as the only two endpoints that accepted stdio command/args/env in the request body pre-1.83.7. Any POST to these paths is a high-fidelity exploit signal. Cross-checked Horizon3.ai write-up and BerriAI security advisory. Defender Advanced Hunting has no clean inbound-HTTP request table, so defender_kql left empty; primary surface is reverse-proxy / IIS / WAF logs (sentinel_kql + datadog_query). Cross-checked against: • https://www.horizon3.ai/ • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pen-test or vulnerability scanner (Tenable, Qualys, Nuclei) probing for CVE-2026-42271
  • Internal admin testing MCP server configuration via the preview workflow before save (legitimate pre-1.83.7 usage)
  • Post-patch admin role traffic to the same URI (now PROXY_ADMIN-gated — verify role binding)
  • Synthetic monitoring (Datadog Synthetics, Pingdom) hitting LiteLLM endpoints that happen to share the path prefix
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<known scanner CIDRs>", "<internal admin CIDRs>")
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","qualys","tenable","DatadogSynthetics")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull source IP, auth header / csUserName, and request body if logged; check the body for `command`, `args`, `env` JSON keys, and confirm LiteLLM version < 1.83.7 on the target. 2) Contain: block both URIs at the reverse proxy / WAF, rotate the proxy master key and every model-provider API key stored by LiteLLM, restart the LiteLLM container to kill any spawned subprocesses. 3) Hunt: on the LiteLLM host pivot to DeviceProcessEvents where InitiatingProcessFileName has python/uvicorn within ±5 minutes of each POST (UC2 logic), pull all outbound from the host since the first POST, check for new ASEP / cron entries and reads of /root/.aws, .env or kubeconfig.

LiteLLM proxy (uvicorn/python) spawning shell or LOLBin — CVE-2026-42271 post-exploit AIInstallation High
Detects child processes spawned by the LiteLLM proxy process (python/uvicorn running litellm) where the child is a shell, network downloader, or recon binary inconsistent with normal LiteLLM operation. CVE-2026-42271 spawns the attacker-supplied command as a subprocess of the proxy process — this is the host-side fingerprint of successful exploitation. Rationale: BerriAI's advisory and the article both state the proxy 'spawned the supplied command as a subprocess on the proxy host with the privileges of the proxy process'. The parent process is therefore python/uvicorn running litellm.proxy. Any shell / curl / whoami child of that exact parent is the canonical post-exploit fingerprint and rare in normal LiteLLM operation. Cross-checked BerriAI advisory and Horizon3.ai analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://www.horizon3.ai/ • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM custom callback / plugin shelling out to `curl` for webhook delivery or to `aws`/`gcloud` for cloud-key resolution
  • DB migration script running `alembic upgrade` or `prisma migrate` at container start (parent uvicorn -> bash -> migrate)
  • Health-check / readiness probe running `whoami` or `id` for diagnostics
  • Pen-test or red-team intentionally exercising CVE-2026-42271 against a staging deployment
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("alembic upgrade","prisma migrate","pip install","--health","healthcheck")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--health","migrate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full ProcessCommandLine of the child, InitiatingProcessId, and the connecting RemoteIP from DeviceNetworkEvents within ±60s. Confirm LiteLLM version < 1.83.7 on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender / Falcon network containment, stop the LiteLLM container, rotate every secret stored by the proxy (model provider API keys, DB creds, SSO secrets) and any cloud IAM role attached to the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of the same LiteLLM PID for the last 7d, all outbound DNS / network connects from the proxy process, new ASEP / cron / systemd unit writes, and reads of /root/.aws, /root/.kube, .env or model-key files. Pivot to other LiteLLM hosts in the fleet for the same parent->child shape.

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("litellm","litellm.proxy","litellm.main","--port 4000")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat","nslookup","dig","whoami","id","uname","chmod","base64")

Anomalous Host header to LiteLLM (Starlette CVE-2026-48710 BadHost bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP requests to LiteLLM that carry a Host header outside the deployment's baseline of expected hosts, especially when reaching auth-gated paths. CVE-2026-48710 abuses Starlette's host header validation so an attacker can submit a forged Host to bypass LiteLLM's auth and reach the vulnerable MCP test endpoints unauthenticated. Rationale: Horizon3.ai chained CVE-2026-48710 (Starlette BadHost) with CVE-2026-42271 to reach LiteLLM's MCP test endpoints unauthenticated, and the article's mitigation guidance explicitly calls out reviewing logs for 'unusual Host header activity'. The on-wire signature is a request whose Host header is forged or unexpected for the deployment. Defender / Falcon FDR don't ship HTTP request data so those fields are empty; primary surface is HTTP access logs. Cross-checked Horizon3.ai analysis and Starlette security advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.horizon3.ai/ • https://github.com/encode/starlette/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal scanner or load balancer health probe sending an IP-literal Host header instead of the DNS name
  • New legitimate LiteLLM hostname added to the deployment that isn't yet in the 30d baseline
  • Kubernetes ingress / service mesh sidecar (Istio, Linkerd) rewriting Host on internal traffic
  • Developer hitting LiteLLM via `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` while debugging in a non-prod environment
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !in ("localhost","127.0.0.1","<known internal probe hosts>")
| where CIp !startswith "10."  // tune to your private ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the Host value, source IP and full URI; confirm Starlette version ≤ 1.0.0 in the LiteLLM deployment's dependency tree (`pip show starlette`); check whether the source IP is inside the corporate perimeter or external. 2) Contain: front LiteLLM with a strict Host allowlist at the reverse proxy / WAF and drop unknown Host values; upgrade Starlette to ≥ 1.0.1 and LiteLLM to ≥ 1.83.7; rotate model provider keys and proxy admin tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the LiteLLM host's DeviceProcessEvents / ProcessRollup2 for python/uvicorn parents spawning shells in the same window (UC2), and pull all outbound network from the LiteLLM host since the first anomalous Host header to look for credential exfil.
// Targets Azure App Service deployments of LiteLLM (AppServiceHTTPLogs carries CsHost).
// For IIS-fronted / WAF-fronted deployments, pull Host from the upstream WAF custom field.
let Baseline = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1h))
    | summarize by _ResourceId, CsHost;
AppServiceHTTPLogs

| join kind=leftanti Baseline on _ResourceId, CsHost
| project TimeGenerated, _ResourceId, CsHost, CsMethod, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, CIp, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
