Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Check Point Remote Access VPN inbound auth from CVE-2026-50751 actor VPS IPs AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound IKE/IPSec authentication or SSL VPN login attempts to Check Point Remote Access / Mobile Access gateways from the eight VPS IPs Check Point published as the CVE-2026-50751 / Qilin-affiliate infrastructure. Article-specific because it pivots on the published IOC IP set and on IKEv1 / Mobile Access ports. Rationale: Pivots on the eight VPS IPs Check Point published (article body) and the IKEv1 / Mobile Access ports the bypass requires. Cross-checked with Check Point's own blog and BleepingComputer write-up confirming the same IP set and hosting providers (Vultr, Shock Hosting, Kaupo Cloud HK). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/check-point-releases-important-hotfix-for-vulnerabilities-in-deprecated-ikev1-vpn-protocol/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/08/check-point-cve-2026-50751-qilin-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning vendor (Censys/Shadowserver) probing the gateway from one of the Vultr ranges — same VPS provider, different intent
  • Internal red-team engagement using a Vultr-rented VPS that happens to overlap the IP set
  • Shared-VPS reassignment: the IP gets re-leased to a benign tenant after Check Point's observation window — historical IOC hit on a now-clean tenant
  • An MSP / partner connecting from a Vultr Singapore / HK node that overlaps the listed /24
Suppression filter
// Suppress benign Vultr/Shock hits to gateways that have the patch applied AND machine cert required
| where DeviceName !in~ ((DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has "Check Point" and SoftwareVersion has_any ("R82.10 Take 20","R82 Take 104","R81.20 Take 142") | summarize DeviceName=make_set(DeviceName)))
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the Check Point gateway is in scope (IKEv1 enabled, machine cert NOT required, legacy clients accepted per the four preconditions in the advisory). Pull the VPN session log for the matching source IP: which user account was bound, did the office mode IP get assigned, were post-auth resources accessed. 2) Contain — disable IKEv1 on the gateway and force machine-cert requirement (Check Point's recommended mitigation), kill any live session for that source IP, rotate the password of the impersonated account, isolate any internal host the session touched. 3) Hunt — pivot from any internal IP the session reached: search 30 days back for outbound to the eight actor IPs, for ELF files matching the known Qilin MD5s, and for rclone.exe / rclone executions to cloud storage providers.
// Targets internet-facing CP gateway whose NIC is enrolled in Defender for Endpoint / Server
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)   // Check Point assesses earliest exploitation 2026-05-07
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionInbound")
| where RemoteIP in ("45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167")
| where LocalPort in (500, 4500, 443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
let actorIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Check Point"
| where SourceIP in (actorIPs) or DestinationIP in (actorIPs)
| where DestinationPort in (500, 4500, 443) or Activity has_any ("IKE","VPN","Mobile Access","Remote Access")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Qilin Linux ransomware ELF payload (CVE-2026-50751 campaign) — known MD5 file event AIInstallation Medium
Detects file write, file open, or process execution of a Linux ELF whose MD5 matches one of the two payloads Check Point attributed to the post-VPN-bypass Qilin affiliate stage. Specific to this article because it ships the two MD5 hashes the vendor published. Rationale: Both MD5s are taken verbatim from the article's IOC block and corroborated by Check Point's own advisory (linked to Qilin Linux ELF binaries per the BleepingComputer write-up). High-fidelity — file hashes do not collide with benign software in practice. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/check-point-releases-important-hotfix-for-vulnerabilities-in-deprecated-ikev1-vpn-protocol/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/
ATT&CKT1486 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/forensic analyst intentionally downloading the sample to a sandbox VM that ships telemetry
  • DFIR tool extracting the hash from a memory image and the AV scans the extracted blob
  • Threat-intel platform syncing the sample to a quarantine bucket whose path is on a monitored volume
  • Red-team detonation drill replaying the published IOC for purple-team validation
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm host: is it the VPN gateway itself, a Linux server in the DMZ, or an internal Linux workload? Inspect the parent process (was it dropped by a Check Point process, by SSH, by rclone)? Capture the file before EDR quarantines it. 2) Contain — isolate the host immediately, snapshot the volume for forensics, kill any running ELF process matching the hash, rotate creds for any service account on the host, block egress to the eight actor IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt — pivot from the host to the VPN session that placed the payload: which user account, which source IP, how long was the session active? Search 45 days back for the same MD5 cluster-wide, for rclone exfil to cloud storage from the same host, and for sibling ELF drops in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp.

| order by Timestamp asc

Rclone exfiltration from Check Point VPN gateway or post-bypass internal host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects rclone execution to a remote cloud target from a host that recently terminated a Remote Access VPN session — the exfiltration tradecraft Check Point and BleepingComputer attribute to this Qilin affiliate following CVE-2026-50751. Article-specific because it pairs rclone (named in the external advisories) with the Check Point campaign window. Rationale: Article body names rclone abuse and ELF download from actor-controlled infra in the post-exploit phase; cross-checked with Check Point's blog and BleepingComputer's write-up which both explicitly call out rclone. The combination of rclone binary + transfer verb + cloud remote prefix is the published tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/check-point-releases-important-hotfix-for-vulnerabilities-in-deprecated-ikev1-vpn-protocol/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin using rclone to sync backups to S3/B2 nightly under a known service account
  • DevOps pipeline pushing build artifacts to GCS via rclone
  • Personal use of rclone copy to OneDrive / Drive by power-user developer
  • Cloud-migration project shipping bulk archives to azureblob:
Suppression filter
// Suppress sanctioned backup automation
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("cron","systemd","jenkins","gitlab-runner","ansible-playbook")
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc_backup","svc_rclone_prod")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the parent process tree and the user context. If the parent is a shell spawned by sshd, an interactive session, or a Check Point VPN daemon process, treat as malicious. Inspect rclone config (~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf) for the remote target and credentials — capture before the actor purges them. Identify volume transferred (network egress bytes during the rclone runtime). 2) Contain — kill the rclone process, block egress to the resolved cloud-storage endpoint at the firewall, isolate the host, revoke any cloud-storage IAM keys discovered in the rclone config, rotate service-account creds on the host. 3) Hunt — pivot to the host's recent inbound VPN sessions for matches to the eight actor IPs, search 45 days back for other hosts running rclone with the same remote name, and check the cloud-storage provider's logs for upload events from the configured remote.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where FileName =~ "rclone" or FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brclone\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","move","copyto","moveto","cat")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s(mega|s3|b2|drive|dropbox|onedrive|pcloud|box|gcs|azureblob|webdav|sftp|ftp|remote):"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/|\\)rclone(\.exe)?$" or TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|/|\\)rclone(\.exe)?$" or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brclone\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","move","copyto","moveto","cat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s(mega|s3|b2|drive|dropbox|onedrive|pcloud|box|gcs|azureblob|webdav|sftp|ftp|remote):"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internal host outbound to CVE-2026-50751 Qilin actor IPs (post-bypass C2 / staging) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections from any internal host to the eight VPS IPs Check Point published — i.e. an inside-out beacon or staging callback after the VPN gateway was compromised. Article-specific because the IPs are the exact post-exploit infrastructure named in the IOC block. Rationale: All eight IPs taken directly from the article IOC block; the BleepingComputer and Check Point sources confirm these are the actor-controlled VPS nodes used for both the bypass and post-exploit ELF staging. Outbound to a known-bad IP set is one of the cleanest signal shapes in detection engineering. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/check-point-releases-important-hotfix-for-vulnerabilities-in-deprecated-ikev1-vpn-protocol/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/08/attackers-had-month-long-head-start-on-patched-check-point-vpn-zero-day/5252438
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion tool reaching out to enrich the same IPs (Censys/VirusTotal/Shodan agents on a SOC analyst workstation)
  • Internal red-team / purple-team test using a Vultr VM that overlaps the IOC range
  • TI feed validation: a SIEM connector resolving the IPs to test reachability
  • Vultr-hosted SaaS the org legitimately uses whose IP rotates onto one of these addresses post-actor-retirement
Suppression filter
// Suppress SOC analyst workstations that legitimately enrich IOCs
| where DeviceName !in~ ("soc-analyst-01","soc-analyst-02","ti-enrichment-host")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("censys.exe","shodan.exe","vt-cli.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage — identify the source host, the initiating process (Sysmon/Defender InitiatingProcessFileName), and whether the egress was DNS-resolved or hardcoded. Pull egress bytes — a large outbound transfer suggests rclone staging; a small periodic conn suggests beaconing. 2) Contain — block all eight IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host, snapshot it, kill the initiating process, and revoke any credentials present on the host. 3) Hunt — pivot to the host's recent inbound VPN session (search CommonSecurityLog with DeviceVendor='Check Point' bound to its assigned office-mode IP), look for sibling internal hosts contacting the same IPs in the 45-day window, and check for the two known MD5s and rclone executions on the same host.
let actorIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFound")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteIP in (actorIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), ConnCount = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 20), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen asc

ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where DstIpAddr in (actorIPs)
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sessions = count(), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber, 20), Hosts = make_set(SrcHostname, 50) by DstIpAddr, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by FirstSeen asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs

| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486

DeviceFileEvents

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI brands as bait: How threat actors are using the AI hype in social engineering

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-08 17 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

As threat actors operationalize AI to accelerate attacks, they are also leveraging the wider global interest around AI itself as a social engineering lure. The post AI brands as bait: How threat actors are using the AI hype in social engineering appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ChatGPT Plus payment-update phishing emails (display-name + subject lure) · [LLM] Claude 'Appeal Request' phishing email with PDF attachment lure · [LLM] Phishing redirect chain via awstrack.me / Rebrandly into AI-themed landing path · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AI brands as bait: How threat actors are using the AI hype in social engineering
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Connection to AI-brand phishing / installer C2 infrastructure (MSTI June 2026 IOCs) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

ChatGPT Plus payment-update phishing emails (display-name + subject lure) AIDelivery High
Detects the Microsoft-tracked ChatGPT-themed credential/credit-card phishing wave (4,500 emails to South Africa on 5 May 2026, peaking 100k/day across CH/AT/ZA) that impersonates OpenAI billing with the urgent 'update your payment method or downgrade' lure. Pivots on the verbatim sender display name and subject pattern the campaign uses. Rationale: Pulls the campaign's two strongest invariants: SenderDisplayName 'ChatGPT' and the verbatim Subject token 'ChatGPT Plus' co-occurring with the urgency-lure words ('payment method', 'continues to work', 'downgraded', 'free plan') quoted in the MSTI write-up. Excludes the real openai.com sending domain to drop legitimate billing.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness team forwarding a sample of the phish internally for training
  • Legitimate OpenAI dunning emails (caught by the openai.com sender-domain filter)
  • Customer-support reply chains that quote the original phish subject
  • Third-party billing aggregators that reuse the 'Plus subscription' phrasing
  • Newsletters/blog digests embedding the lure as a screenshot/text quote
Suppression filter
and SenderFromDomain !endswith "openai.com" and SenderFromDomain !endswith "stripe.com" and not (SenderFromAddress has_any ("phishtest","awareness","knowbe4"))
Response runbook
Triage: review SenderFromAddress, SenderIPv4, and UrlDomain on the matching EmailEvents row; confirm the URL chain does not terminate at openai.com or stripe.com. Contain: soft-delete and add the sender + URL domain to the org tenant block list via Defender for O365 Tenant Allow/Block list; trigger AIR investigation for in-mailbox copies. Hunt: pivot on UrlClickEvents over the past 30 days for the matching NetworkMessageId / UrlChain, then on DeviceProcessEvents for any process spawned within 60s of the click on affected hosts to spot credential-harvest follow-through.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (SenderDisplayName =~ "ChatGPT" or SenderFromAddress has "chatgpt")
    and Subject has "ChatGPT Plus"
    and Subject has_any ("payment method","continues to work","update your payment","downgraded","free plan")
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "openai.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Subject has "ChatGPT Plus" and Subject has_any ("payment method","continues to work","update your payment","downgraded","free plan")
| where tostring(P2Sender) !endswith "openai.com"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Subject, Sender = tostring(P2Sender), Recipients = tostring(P2RecipientList), MessageId = tostring(InternetMessageId), Operation
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude 'Appeal Request' phishing email with PDF attachment lure AIDelivery High
Detects the Anthropic-impersonating phishing wave (20-22 Apr 2026, 2000+ orgs, primarily US/UK/IN tech sector) that uses the display names 'Anthropic Teams' / 'Anthropic PBC', a 'Claude Appeal Request' subject, and a 'Fill and Sign Claude Appeal Form.pdf' attachment carrying the AiTM credential-harvest link to dash.awaydouble[.]org. Rationale: Three article-specific high-fidelity tokens: the verbatim attachment FileName 'Fill and Sign Claude Appeal Form.pdf', the SenderDisplayName values 'Anthropic Teams' / 'Anthropic PBC', and the 'Claude Appeal Request' Subject. The PDF filename alone is essentially zero-FP. The display-name + subject combo is the fallback for renamed attachments. Anti-AiTM lure (dash.awaydouble[.]org) is covered separately in UC3.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656 T1557
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal awareness team forwarding the captured sample as training material
  • Legitimate Anthropic trust-and-safety enforcement emails (filtered via anthropic.com domain)
  • Customer-support escalation threads quoting the lure subject
  • Legal/compliance teams forwarding the phish to internal counsel
  • Security-vendor breach-report digests embedding the lure as a screenshot
Suppression filter
and SenderFromDomain !endswith "anthropic.com" and not (SenderFromAddress has_any ("phishtest","awareness","knowbe4","@<your-soc-mailbox>"))
Response runbook
Triage: confirm SenderFromDomain is not anthropic.com and check whether the embedded PDF link resolves to dash.awaydouble[.]org or another non-Anthropic domain. Contain: soft-delete + zap all mailbox copies via Defender AIR; add the SenderFromAddress and IP to tenant block list; force token-revoke + password reset for any RecipientEmailAddress whose mailbox shows the message opened or attachment clicked. Hunt: query UrlClickEvents for clicks on dash.awaydouble[.]org / awaydouble[.]org over the past 60 days and SigninLogs for the same UPN for non-compliant-device or anomalous-country sign-ins in the click + 24h window — classic AiTM token-theft pattern.
let suspect_mail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SenderDisplayName in~ ("Anthropic Teams","Anthropic PBC")
         or Subject matches regex @"(?i)Claude\s+Appeal\s+Request"
    | where SenderFromDomain !endswith "anthropic.com";
let suspect_attach = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileType =~ "pdf"
    | where FileName =~ "Fill and Sign Claude Appeal Form.pdf"
         or FileName matches regex @"(?i)(Claude|Anthropic).{0,20}Appeal.{0,20}Form.*\.pdf$";
suspect_mail
| join kind=inner suspect_attach on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Subject matches regex @"(?i)Claude\s+Appeal\s+Request"
    or tostring(ItemAttachments) has "Fill and Sign Claude Appeal Form.pdf"
| where tostring(P2Sender) !endswith "anthropic.com"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Subject, Sender = tostring(P2Sender), Recipients = tostring(P2RecipientList), Attachments = tostring(ItemAttachments), MessageId = tostring(InternetMessageId)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Connection to AI-brand phishing / installer C2 infrastructure (MSTI June 2026 IOCs) AICommand & Control High
Network-side detection for the eight Microsoft-published domains backing the ChatGPT/Claude AiTM landing pages and the fake DeepSeek/Manus/Seedance installer C2. Fires on any DNS resolution or HTTP egress to the IOC set; high-fidelity because these are dedicated attacker infrastructure with no known legitimate use. Rationale: Eight domains explicitly attributed by Microsoft Threat Intelligence to this campaign: legendarytrendsbay.shop (ChatGPT phish landing), dash.awaydouble.org / awaydouble.org (Claude AiTM landing), and the four installer-C2 domains. Detection is a literal IOC match — appropriate for alerting tier because attribution is high-confidence and the domains have no legitimate business use.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst manually visiting the IOC for triage (filter on known-analyst workstations)
  • Sandbox / detonation chamber egress to the IOCs during sample analysis
  • Threat-intel scanner (Recorded Future, VirusTotal Hunting) crawling the IOC
  • Browser prefetch / DoH safety check resolving the domain without a real visit
  • Email security product following the redirect chain for verdict determination (e.g. Defender Safe Links scan)
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("<known-analyst-account>") and DeviceName !in~ ("<sandbox-host-list>")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName (browser vs LOLBin vs unknown installer) on the affected DeviceName and whether the URL path contained /ChatGPT/ (phish lure) or pointed at a binary payload. Contain: block the eight domains at perimeter DNS/proxy AND in Defender Indicators; isolate the device via Defender LiveResponse if the calling process was anything other than a browser visiting the phish landing. Hunt: pivot DeviceProcessEvents for the same DeviceId across the past 14 days for any of the lure executables (deepseek-v4-*_x64.exe etc.) and for SigninLogs MFA-challenge / anomalous-token events on the logged-on user post-visit (AiTM token theft).
let ioc_domains = dynamic(["legendarytrendsbay.shop","dash.awaydouble.org","awaydouble.org","servicing.pureplantcravings.com","pureplantcravings.com","brokeapt.com","pan.ssffaa19.xyz","ssffaa19.xyz"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where host in (ioc_domains)
    or RemoteUrl has_any (ioc_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, host, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let ioc_domains = dynamic(["legendarytrendsbay.shop","dash.awaydouble.org","awaydouble.org","servicing.pureplantcravings.com","pureplantcravings.com","brokeapt.com","pan.ssffaa19.xyz","ssffaa19.xyz"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where tolower(DnsQuery) in (ioc_domains) or DnsQuery has_any (ioc_domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, EventVendor, EventProduct, EventKind = "dns"),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where Url has_any (ioc_domains) or DstHostname in (ioc_domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, Url), EventVendor, EventProduct, EventKind = "web"),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where DestinationHostName has_any (ioc_domains) or RequestURL has_any (ioc_domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcUsername = SourceUserName, Indicator = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), EventVendor = DeviceVendor, EventProduct = DeviceProduct, EventKind = "firewall")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 2d4a9b6e-3c2d-4f7a-b8e1-7a0c1e9d4f55
description: Detects DNS or HTTP egress to the eight Microsoft Threat Intelligence-published domains backing the ChatGPT/Claude AiTM landing pages and fake AI installer C2.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:
  selection:

      - 'dash.awaydouble.org'
      - 'awaydouble.org'
      - 'servicing.pureplantcravings.com'

(source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:(3 OR 22) AND (@DestinationHostname:(legendarytrendsbay.shop OR dash.awaydouble.org OR awaydouble.org OR servicing.pureplantcravings.com OR pureplantcravings.com OR brokeapt.com OR pan.ssffaa19.xyz OR ssffaa19.xyz) OR @QueryName:(legendarytrendsbay.shop OR dash.awaydouble.org OR awaydouble.org OR servicing.pureplantcravings.com OR pureplantcravings.com OR brokeapt.com OR pan.ssffaa19.xyz OR ssffaa19.xyz))) OR (source:(zscaler OR paloalto OR fortinet OR cisco_umbrella) AND @url:(*legendarytrendsbay.shop* OR *awaydouble.org* OR *pureplantcravings.com* OR *brokeapt.com* OR *ssffaa19.xyz*))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| DomainName=/^(legendarytrendsbay\.shop|dash\.awaydouble\.org|awaydouble\.org|servicing\.pureplantcravings\.com|pureplantcravings\.com|brokeapt\.com|pan\.ssffaa19\.xyz|ssffaa19\.xyz)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("legendarytrendsbay.shop","dash.awaydouble.org","awaydouble.org","servicing.pureplantcravings.com","pureplantcravings.com","brokeapt.com","pan.ssffaa19.xyz","ssffaa19.xyz")) by All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Execution or drop of fake AI-platform installer (DeepSeek/Manus/Seedance/GPT-5.5/Kimi) AIInstallation High
Detects the malicious installer binaries Storm-3075 ships through SEO-poisoned GitHub repos masquerading as AI tools (DeepSeek-V4, Manus AI, Seedance, GPT-5.5, Kimi-Swarm). Combines verbatim filename match, the eight MSTI-published SHA256 hashes, and a permissive regex pattern keyed on the consistent '*_x64.exe' naming convention dropped into Downloads/Temp. Rationale: Three layers of fidelity: (1) verbatim FileName match for the seven binaries enumerated in MSTI's lure-table (rows 2-6); (2) hash-equal on all eight published SHA256 IOCs — zero-FP even if the file is renamed; (3) regex on the campaign's consistent '*_x64.exe' naming convention scoped to Downloads/Temp/Public to catch future siblings dropped from the same MSaaS signing pipeline. Article explicitly notes Storm-3075 uses these names through fake GitHub orgs (DeepSeek-V4, ManusAI-agent, bytedance-seedance).
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1608.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DeepSeek / ByteDance Seedance / Moonshot Kimi installer downloaded from the official vendor site (distinguishable via publisher cert: vendor-signed not MSaaS-signed)
  • Security researcher detonating samples in a corp-attached sandbox VM
  • IT redistributing the genuine open-source AI model launcher to dev workstations
  • Renamed in-house tool that accidentally matches the naming regex (e.g. 'kimi-swarm-station' if your firm runs an internal swarm orchestrator)
  • Threat-hunting team replaying historical IOCs as part of detection-engineering validation
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\<dfs-share>\\\\Software\\\\")) and DeviceName !in~ ("<sandbox-host-list>")
Response runbook
Triage: pull SHA256 + publisher cert details for the matching ProcessId; if hash is on the MSTI list, treat as confirmed Storm-3075. Check ParentImage — Downloads-folder browser parent confirms SEO-poisoning vector; cmd/PowerShell parent suggests script-stage. Contain: isolate the host via Defender LiveResponse, kill the process, hash-block the SHA256 tenant-wide in Defender Indicators, revoke the user's Azure AD refresh tokens. Hunt: look for the same SHA256 / FileName across the whole estate (DeviceFileEvents), pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the affected host to the IOC domains in UC3 for the past 30 days, and review the user's browser history / EmailUrlInfo for the GitHub-repo SEO landing.
let lure_binaries = dynamic(["deepseek-v4-pro_x64.exe","deepseek-v4-flash_x64.exe","Manus_AI_Desktop_x64.exe","seedance_x64.exe","gpt-5.5-Pro_x64.exe","gpt-5.5-Thinking_x64.exe","Kimi-Swarm-Station_x64.exe"]);
let ioc_sha256 = dynamic(["791efb555eefb7215e96659a1353a97416743b66bdd72705493129c64057d40e","c7c5072df9f83f4c440a5c3bb4be1d5f6c67bbf78f196406ca20d27b43b975b8","0a26238f6c516de5885457c93042531aa59bc206a9537cebf5267cedc6c68531","8610d4fb0ec5b525071c2aaec4df0f8fcbb3673aba58a7e1959fc44e83c0e2ca","99231deb373997364381d1eb513d2d42231d418c3a2db9007c5af9bd56ab9371","25270cc429ada8028b5b33220ed412c47907ecceea7377d608fac5af01bed56a","56d722b0331bf0aaa86bb37483486c6dff6ad9427fc473ed7c3226c21a9bdd23","5455341ed1bbe75a664fca2dd0794c508e1874f75360253a7ff5bc119bc92d80"]);
let ai_lure_regex = @"(?i)^(deepseek-v\d+(-pro|-flash)?|manus_ai_desktop|seedance|gpt-\d+(\.\d+)?-(pro|thinking)|kimi-swarm-station)_x64\.exe$";
union isfuzzy=false
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
        | where FileName in~ (lure_binaries)
            or SHA256 in (ioc_sha256)
            or (FileName matches regex ai_lure_regex and FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\",@"\Temp\",@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",@"\Public\"))
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EvtKind = "process", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
        | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
        | where FileName in~ (lure_binaries) or SHA256 in (ioc_sha256)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, EvtKind = "file", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessParentFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let lure_binaries = dynamic(["deepseek-v4-pro_x64.exe","deepseek-v4-flash_x64.exe","Manus_AI_Desktop_x64.exe","seedance_x64.exe","gpt-5.5-Pro_x64.exe","gpt-5.5-Thinking_x64.exe","Kimi-Swarm-Station_x64.exe"]);
let ioc_sha256 = dynamic(["791efb555eefb7215e96659a1353a97416743b66bdd72705493129c64057d40e","c7c5072df9f83f4c440a5c3bb4be1d5f6c67bbf78f196406ca20d27b43b975b8","0a26238f6c516de5885457c93042531aa59bc206a9537cebf5267cedc6c68531","8610d4fb0ec5b525071c2aaec4df0f8fcbb3673aba58a7e1959fc44e83c0e2ca","99231deb373997364381d1eb513d2d42231d418c3a2db9007c5af9bd56ab9371","25270cc429ada8028b5b33220ed412c47907ecceea7377d608fac5af01bed56a","56d722b0331bf0aaa86bb37483486c6dff6ad9427fc473ed7c3226c21a9bdd23","5455341ed1bbe75a664fca2dd0794c508e1874f75360253a7ff5bc119bc92d80"]);
let ai_lure_regex = @"(?i)(deepseek-v\d+(-pro|-flash)?|manus_ai_desktop|seedance|gpt-\d+(\.\d+)?-(pro|thinking)|kimi-swarm-station)_x64\.exe";
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where tolower(ActingProcessName) has_any (lure_binaries)
            or SHA256 in (ioc_sha256)
            or ActingProcessName matches regex ai_lure_regex
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EvtKind="process", ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256),
    (SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d) and EventID == 4688
        | where tolower(NewProcessName) has_any (lure_binaries)
            or NewProcessName matches regex ai_lure_regex
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=Computer, ActorUsername=SubjectUserName, EvtKind="process", ActingProcessName=NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine=CommandLine, SHA256=FileHash)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing redirect chain via awstrack.me / Rebrandly into AI-themed landing path AIDelivery Medium
Detects user clicks on the multi-hop redirect chain Storm-3075/affiliates use to launder phish URLs: legit CRM (bitrix24) → Amazon awstrack.me email-tracking → Rebrandly short link → compromised legendarytrendsbay[.]shop /ChatGPT/ path (or sibling AI-themed paths). Targets the SHAPE of the chain (awstrack.me forwarding into an AI-brand path), not just static IOCs, so it also catches campaign rotation. Rationale: Two pivot shapes from the MSTI ChatGPT-phish attack chain: (1) literal IOC match on the six known phish landings; (2) behavioural pattern of a click through awstrack.me/Rebrandly/bitrix24 that terminates at a path containing an AI-brand token — this is the exact funnel diagrammed in Figure 1 and survives URL rotation since the AI-brand path component is the lure invariant. Path-regex /(ChatGPT|Claude|Anthropic|DeepSeek)/ also catches the article's note that the threat actor placed phishing pages in a /ChatGPT/ folder on compromised legendarytrendsbay[.]shop.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1656
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing or sales team using Bitrix24 CRM legitimately, with AWS SES tracking and an AI-themed campaign name in the URL
  • Legitimate Anthropic / OpenAI newsletter using Rebrandly short links (verify the terminal landing is the genuine vendor domain)
  • Security awareness training that simulates this exact lure (Defender Attack Simulator may surface here)
  • Procurement team evaluating an AI vendor demo via a shortened URL containing the vendor name
  • Internal employee blog post embedding a Rebrandly link that references an AI tool
Suppression filter
and AccountUpn !in~ ("<known-marketing-accounts>") and not (UrlChain has "openai.com" or UrlChain has "anthropic.com" or UrlChain has "deepseek.com")
Response runbook
Triage: inspect the full UrlChain field — confirm the chain terminates at a non-vendor domain (legendarytrendsbay[.]shop, awaydouble[.]org, etc.) not openai.com / anthropic.com / deepseek.com. Pull EmailUrlInfo by the matching NetworkMessageId to identify the originating phish. Contain: revoke active sessions for the AccountUpn via Entra ID risky-user workflow; add Conditional Access requirement for re-MFA on next sign-in; block the terminal landing domain at proxy. Hunt: SigninLogs for the same UPN looking for unfamiliar-location or device-not-compliant sign-ins in the click + 4h window (AiTM token theft); EmailEvents for siblings of the same campaign that hit other recipients.
let phish_landings = dynamic(["legendarytrendsbay.shop","dash.awaydouble.org","awaydouble.org","servicing.pureplantcravings.com","pureplantcravings.com","brokeapt.com"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| where Url has_any (phish_landings)
    or UrlChain has_any (phish_landings)
    or (Url has_any ("awstrack.me","rebrand.ly","rebrandly.com","bitrix24.com") and Url matches regex @"(?i)(chatgpt|claude|anthropic|deepseek|manus|seedance|gpt-?5|kimi)")
    or Url matches regex @"(?i)https?://[^/]+/(ChatGPT|Claude|Anthropic|DeepSeek)/"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlChain, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload
| order by Timestamp desc

    or Url matches regex @"(?i)https?://[^/]+/(ChatGPT|Claude|Anthropic|DeepSeek)/"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
