Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] iOS device exposed to CVE-2026-47430 (cordova-plugin-inappbrowser 3.1.0–6.0.0) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Developer workstation installs vulnerable cordova-plugin-inappbrowser version (CVE-2026-47430)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
iOS device exposed to CVE-2026-47430 (cordova-plugin-inappbrowser 3.1.0–6.0.0) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces enrolled iOS endpoints whose vulnerability scanner reports CVE-2026-47430 — i.e. they have an installed app shipping cordova-plugin-inappbrowser in the 3.1.0 through 6.0.0 range. Drives patch prioritisation: any app on the list is exploitable by any URL it loads in its InAppBrowser (OAuth redirect, marketing link, deep-link target). Rationale: Pure asset-exposure hunt anchored on the article's exact CVE ID (CVE-2026-47430) and affected version range (3.1.0–6.0.0, fixed in 6.0.1). The TVM branch is high-fidelity once Microsoft ships coverage; the inventory branch parses the version string so it fires immediately on day-zero. Cross-checked against vulnerability.circl.lu listing for CVE-2026-47430 and the Apache Cordova InAppBrowser 6.0.1 release announcement. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/cve-2026-47430 • https://cordova.apache.org/blog/ • http://www.mail-archive.com/issues@cordova.apache.org/msg132193.html
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test / sandbox iOS devices intentionally pinned to an older Cordova version for regression testing
  • Internal app held back from the 6.0.1 bump pending QA — flagged correctly but already known to the mobile team
  • Inventory-branch parsing misses a non-semver tag (e.g. '6.0.0-beta.2') and skips a device that is in fact vulnerable
  • DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory lag (>24h) showing devices that already updated
  • Third-party MDM not enrolled in Defender so the device shows up empty rather than vulnerable (false negative, not FP, but worth flagging)
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.0.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "7."
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the device list, group by SoftwareName + owning app team, and confirm against MDM whether the impacted apps are first-party, third-party-vendor, or store apps. First-party is fixable today; vendor apps go to the vendor-management queue. Step 2 — Contain: push a Conditional Access / Intune compliance policy that blocks the impacted app version on managed devices until upgraded to 6.0.1+; for store apps that can't be pinned, advise users to update from the App Store. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for the affected DeviceIds for the prior 30 days looking at any URL loaded via the impacted app's bundle ID to spot the realistic exploit vector — attacker-controlled OAuth redirect or marketing link. Open a tracking ticket on each non-patched app until SoftwareVersion >= 6.0.1.
// Defender Vulnerability Management surfaces CVE-2026-47430 once Microsoft publishes coverage; the version-range hunt below is the fallback.
let AffectedByCve = DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-47430"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, Source="TVM-CVE";
let AffectedByVersion = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SoftwareName has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser"
    | extend Major = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)\.", 1, SoftwareVersion)),
             Minor = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)\.", 1, SoftwareVersion)),
             Patch = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
    | where (Major >= 3 and Major <= 5)
         or (Major == 3 and Minor >= 1)
         or (Major == 6 and Minor == 0 and Patch == 0)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel="High", RecommendedSecurityUpdate="Upgrade cordova-plugin-inappbrowser to >= 6.0.1", Source="Inventory-VersionRange";
union AffectedByCve, AffectedByVersion
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| where OSPlatform startswith "iOS" or OSPlatform == ""  // iOS-only impact; blank kept for npm-package inventory on dev macs
| order by Timestamp desc
let AffectedByCve = DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-47430"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, Source="TVM-CVE";
let InventoryDevices = DeviceInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, OSVersion, DeviceName) by DeviceId;
AffectedByCve
| join kind=leftouter InventoryDevices on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION

Developer workstation installs vulnerable cordova-plugin-inappbrowser version (CVE-2026-47430) AIWeaponization Medium
Catches a developer or CI runner installing cordova-plugin-inappbrowser pinned to a vulnerable version (3.x, 4.x, 5.x or 6.0.0) via npm/yarn/pnpm. Pre-empts the next build that would ship the vulnerable plugin into a mobile app bundle — i.e. fixes the issue at the supply-chain edge rather than waiting for it to land in the asset inventory. Rationale: Uses the article's exact package name (cordova-plugin-inappbrowser) and the affected-version range explicitly stated in the advisory (3.1.0 through 6.0.0, fixed in 6.0.1). The regex pins the version specifier to a known-vulnerable major/minor so a developer typing the patched 6.0.1 or later won't fire. Cross-checked against vulnerability.circl.lu and the Apache Cordova 6.0.1 release announcement to confirm the patched version string. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/cve-2026-47430 • https://cordova.apache.org/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile-app developer reproducing the CVE on purpose for a security ticket
  • Regression test in CI deliberately installing 6.0.0 to confirm the fix works on 6.0.1
  • Lockfile-resolved transitive install where the repo's package-lock.json still references 5.x — legitimate but should be addressed
  • Build agent on a feature branch that hasn't yet rebased the bump-to-6.0.1 commit
  • A `package.json` in a tutorial / sample repo cloned by a dev to learn Cordova
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\sample" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\test" and not (ProcessCommandLine has "--dry-run" or ProcessCommandLine has "--save=false")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the user and the repo. Pull the parent commandline / current working directory to find which project is pinning the vulnerable spec; check the repo's package.json + package-lock.json in source control. Step 2 — Contain: if this is a production app, open a P1 dependency-bump PR to >= 6.0.1, gate any build artefact from that branch in the CI pipeline, and notify the mobile release manager. If this is exploratory / a fork, attach to the existing tracking ticket. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the parent repo to enumerate other developers who recently checked out the same branch (DeviceFileEvents on package-lock.json modifications), and pull DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for any already-shipped builds that still carry the vulnerable plugin (links to the asset-exposure UC).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","npm","yarn","pnpm","npx.cmd","npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i "," i@")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add ")
| extend VulnerableSpec = extract(@"cordova-plugin-inappbrowser@(?:\^|~)?((?:3\.[1-9][0-9]*|4\.\d+|5\.\d+|6\.0\.0)(?:\.\d+)?)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(VulnerableSpec)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, VulnerableSpec
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm","npx")
   or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "cordova-plugin-inappbrowser"
| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("install"," add "," i ")
| extend VulnerableSpec = extract(@"cordova-plugin-inappbrowser@(?:\^|~)?((?:3\.[1-9][0-9]*|4\.\d+|5\.\d+|6\.0\.0)(?:\.\d+)?)", 1, Cmd)
| where isnotempty(VulnerableSpec)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, Cmd, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, VulnerableSpec
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VerdantBamboo Deploys BSD Variant of BRICKSTORM on Linux Appliances

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A China-nexus cyber espionage group has been observed deploying a BSD variant of a known backdoor called BRICKSTORM, as well as two other malware families codenamed PLENET (aka GRIMBOLT) and AGENTPSD to target Linux systems. The activity has been attributed by Volexity to a threat cluster it tracks as VerdantBamboo, which it said overlaps with hacking groups known as Clay Typhoon (Microsoft),

Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] M365 / Entra sign-ins sourced from BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 · [LLM] Outbound endpoint connections to BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
M365 / Entra sign-ins sourced from BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Microsoft 365 / Entra ID sign-in events whose source IP matches the VerdantBamboo C2 address published by Volexity. Because the actor proxied through compromised Egnyte Storage Sync + pfSense BRICKSTORM SOCKS relays to blend into Conditional Access policies, any direct sign-in from this IP indicates either a misconfigured tunnel or direct actor probing. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the sole IP IOC published by Volexity and reposted by Bleeping Computer / Cybersecuritynews — high-fidelity point IOC. Cross-checked Volexity report and Mallory.ai write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019e9476-afd4-71fe-a6f0-7dff94b7f250
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1090.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel team manually validating the IOC via a proxy from this IP
  • Penetration-test engagement deliberately replaying the IOC
  • Shared NAT environment where the same hosting provider IP is used by a legitimate SaaS the org consumes
  • An incident-response vendor using infrastructure in the same /24 subnet
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Browser")
| where UserAgent !has "Mozilla"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull every SigninLogs row from 149.248.11.71 in the last 30d, capture UPN, AppDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, and SessionId. Cross-reference UserAgent / ClientAppUsed for non-browser tokens (Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, REST). 2) CONTAIN: revoke refresh tokens for every UPN seen (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), force MFA re-enrolment, and add 149.248.11.71 to a Conditional Access named-location block. 3) HUNT: pivot on each affected UPN — search EmailEvents / OfficeActivity for the prior 18 months for mailbox-rule creation, MailItemsAccessed bursts, and OAuth app-consent grants; review SSL VPN logs for sessions matching the same UPN to surface the lateral path from Storage Sync to M365.

| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs

| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ResultType, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM / PLENET / AGENTPSD file-hash IOCs AIInstallation Medium
Point-detection on the eight SHA256, four SHA1 and four MD5 hashes Volexity published for the BSD BRICKSTORM variant, PLENET (.NET AOT) and AGENTPSD (Python reverse shell). Matches across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents so we catch both landing and execution attempts on any Defender-for-Linux / Windows host. Rationale: All 16 hashes published in Volexity's June 2026 Verdant Bamboo blog; cross-checked against the BleepingComputer reposting of the IOC list. Hash detections have negligible FP rate; the broader IOC pivot covers the three malware families (BRICKSTORM BSD, PLENET, AGENTPSD) listed in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://github.com/mandiant/brickstorm-scanner
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1505.003 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / forensic analyst detonating a copy of the sample in a sandbox VM connected to the EDR backbone
  • Threat-intel feed reingest dropping the hash into a TI lookup file the EDR then scans
  • AV product quarantine writing the sample to a vendor-managed quarantine folder
  • Reverse-engineer workstation hosting a deliberately retained copy of the binary
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Quarantine"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull every event for the matching hash and identify the binary's drop path, parent process and signer status. For PLENET / BRICKSTORM samples on Linux/BSD appliances, run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner Bash script against the filesystem to confirm. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host via MDE Machine Isolation (or the appliance equivalent — block at firewall, kill SSH session). Reset credentials cached on the device, especially any service / admin accounts pinned to the Storage Sync / pfSense / NAS appliance. 3) HUNT: pivot every hash hit on its DeviceId across the prior 18 months (the actor's reported dwell time) for AsepValueUpdate / DeviceRegistryEvents persistence, lateral SSH/SMB sessions out of the host, and any M365 OAuth grants under accounts that logged into the host.

AGENTPSD-style Python reverse shell spawned by sshd on Linux / NAS AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the AGENTPSD deployment pattern Volexity describes: VerdantBamboo SSHed into Synology NAS / Linux appliances and dropped a Python-based reverse shell. Surfaces python3 / python processes whose parent is sshd and which subsequently open an outbound socket — a behaviour pattern that survives even when the static hashes mutate. Rationale: The article specifically calls out AGENTPSD as a Python reverse shell deployed over SSH to the Synology NAS. Parent=sshd + child=python is a tight behavioural pair on appliances where Python is rarely launched interactively; the cmd-line tokens are the canonical Python reverse-shell idioms. Cross-checked Volexity blog for the deployment vector (SSH). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chinese-apt-verdantbamboo-uses-brickstorm-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1021.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / SaltStack agentless management running ad-hoc python modules over SSH against Linux fleet
  • DevOps engineer using ssh user@host 'python3 -c ...' for debugging
  • Backup / monitoring agent (e.g. Nagios NRPE-compatible Python plugins) invoked through ssh
  • Synology Active Backup / replication daemon when it spawns python from an sshd context
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in ("ansible","saltstack","nagios","nrpe","backup")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the full ProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername and SrcIpAddr of the originating SSH session; correlate against /var/log/auth.log or DeviceLogonEvents to identify the source IP and account that authenticated. 2) CONTAIN: terminate the python PID, kill the parent sshd session, rotate the credential used (especially shared admin / root accounts on the NAS / pfSense / Storage Sync), and add a deny-from rule for the source IP on the appliance's sshd_config or upstream firewall. 3) HUNT: enumerate sibling files dropped under /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and ~/.cache by the same SSH session; pivot the source IP across NetworkConnectIP4 / VPC flow / firewall logs to see what else it touched; check /etc/cron*, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and systemd unit files for AGENTPSD persistence anchors.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName == "sshd"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python2","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("socket.", "subprocess.", "pty.spawn", "os.dup2", "-c import", "connect((", "/bin/sh", "/bin/bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "sshd"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/python(2|3)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("socket.", "subprocess.", "pty.spawn", "os.dup2", "-c import", "connect((", "/bin/sh", "/bin/bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
title: AGENTPSD-style Python Reverse Shell Spawned by sshd
id: a4127bc8-c5b6-4e5e-b1ec-3f7d4f7c4d31
description: Detects a python interpreter spawned directly by sshd on a Linux / BSD host with command-line arguments matching reverse-shell semantics (socket import, pty.spawn, os.dup2, connect to /bin/sh). Maps to the VerdantBamboo AGENTPSD deployment pattern Volexity documented (June 2026).
references:
  - https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/

  - attack.t1021.004

      - 'subprocess.'
      - '-c import'
      - '/bin/sh'
      - '/bin/bash'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:sshd @process.name:(python OR python2 OR python3) @process.command_line:(*socket.* OR *pty.spawn* OR *os.dup2* OR *subprocess.* OR *"/bin/sh"* OR *"/bin/bash"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin
| ParentBaseFileName=/^sshd$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/python(2|3)?$/i
| regex("(socket\.|pty\.spawn|os\.dup2|subprocess\.|-c import|\/bin\/sh|\/bin\/bash)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Outbound endpoint connections to BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 AICommand & Control Medium
Catches any endpoint, server or appliance making an outbound network connection to the VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM C2 address. Distinct pivot from UC1 (M365 sign-ins) — this targets the BRICKSTORM SOCKS callback channel rather than the resulting Entra session, so it fires even if the proxy never reaches a successful sign-in. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the only network-layer IOC Volexity published. The detection covers every host that BRICKSTORM might call out from (Storage Sync, pfSense, Synology NAS, Windows endpoints) by hitting both EDR and firewall telemetry. Cross-checked Volexity, BleepingComputer and Mallory.ai. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform performing connectivity / sinkhole verification against the published IOC
  • Internal IR sandbox detonating one of the BRICKSTORM samples and reaching the live C2
  • Security researcher / red team simulating the campaign
  • Misconfigured WHOIS / RDAP / passive-DNS enrichment tool that occasionally fetches the IP directly
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe","thehive.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName + DeviceName tuple. If the source is a Linux/BSD appliance (Storage Sync, pfSense, Synology), run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner against the device's filesystem before touching anything. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole 149.248.11.71 at the perimeter firewall (drop, not reset), isolate the originating host, and block the IP/24 at the cloud-egress proxy. 3) HUNT: pivot back ≥18 months (the campaign's documented dwell time) on the same DeviceName for ProcessRollup2 of the BRICKSTORM hashes, AsepValueUpdate persistence, SSH lateral movement to NAS hosts, and any sign-in events from internal SSL VPN-range IPs that correspond temporally to BRICKSTORM heartbeats.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "149.248.11.71"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr == "149.248.11.71"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction, SrcUsername),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "149.248.11.71"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, SourceUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pfSense / firewall config change enabling Web SSL VPN after admin login AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the VerdantBamboo re-entry tactic Volexity documents — after stolen admin credentials let them into the firewall, the actor enabled web SSL VPN access to the appliance and used it for ongoing entry. Surfaces config-write events on the firewall WebGUI / SSL VPN service originating from previously-unseen admin source IPs, correlated to a successful admin login in the preceding 15 minutes. Rationale: Volexity explicitly describes the actor reconnecting to the firewall with stolen admin credentials and then enabling web SSL VPN access on the device — Syslog/php-fpm/configd messages on pfSense are the canonical witness for that change. Defender / Falcon are left empty because pfSense appliances are not typically EDR-instrumented; Sigma is left empty because the correlation requires a time-window join between two log events (rule explicitly forbidden for single-event-shape Sigma). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cyberpress.org/verdantbamboo-breaches-pfsense-firewall/
ATT&CKT1556 T1133 T1078
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate network admin enabling OpenVPN during a maintenance window
  • Vendor MSP performing planned firmware upgrade and re-enabling services
  • Disaster-recovery failover toggling SSL VPN to the secondary HA pair
  • pfBlocker / pfSense plugin update writing to system_advanced_admin during package install
Suppression filter
| where AdminIP !in ("10.10.10.10","192.168.99.5")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the AdminIP from the joined Syslog row and check whether it is a known internal admin jumpbox / NOC IP; review the diff in pfSense config.xml backups (/cf/conf/backup) around ConfigChangeTime. 2) CONTAIN: roll the firewall config back to the previous known-good backup, disable any newly-added OpenVPN server / user/cert, rotate every local pfSense account (especially `admin`), and revoke any newly-issued OpenVPN certificates. 3) HUNT: cross-reference AdminIP against M365 SigninLogs and SSL VPN session logs for the same window; run Mandiant's brickstorm-scanner against the pfSense filesystem; check /var/etc/openvpn/server*/ for unauthorised client certificates and /etc/inc/services.inc for tampered service hooks.
let AdminLogins = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where Facility in ("auth","authpriv") or ProcessName in ("sshd","webConfigurator","php-fpm")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("Successful login for user 'admin'", "Successful webConfigurator login", "Accepted password for admin")
    | extend AdminIP = extract(@"from ([\d\.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | project AdminLoginTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AdminIP;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName in ("php-fpm","configd","check_reload_status","openvpn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("openvpn-server", "server1.conf", "webgui:", "system_advanced_admin", "WebGUI enabled", "User-Manager: 'admin'")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("add","enable","modify","saved")
| join kind=inner AdminLogins on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (AdminLoginTime .. AdminLoginTime + 15m)
| project AdminLoginTime, ConfigChangeTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AdminIP, SyslogMessage
| order by ConfigChangeTime desc
source:linux.syslog @host.name:*pfsense* @process.name:(php-fpm OR configd OR check_reload_status OR openvpn) ("openvpn-server" OR "server1.conf" OR "WebGUI enabled" OR "system_advanced_admin" OR "User-Manager: 'admin'")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the

let BadHashes = dynamic(["ee41e06ed96182ce80cd4544a6abd5d7719c4a5c0e5ddb266a83842d39b99b0a", "40d264cf9c73923932c3dfd52d20f46ff602be3fea8dc6ecc71aca46e6067bf5", "f70abe93121637d3ec2f6c5e058ccac0307ebf63e496f38588cbfc17a8f8a264", "eb141a43958802727a6c813452450c10b92704bea4474ee5fd87c0a1be326e2e", "24a11a26a2586f4fba7bfe89df2e21a0809ad85069e442da98c37c4add369a0c", "dfb37247d12351ef9708cb6631ce2d7017897503657c6b882a711c0da8a9a591", "92fb4ad6dee9362d0596fda7bbcfe1ba353f812ea801d1870e37bfc6376e624a", "aa688682d44f0c6b0ed7f30b981a609100107f2d414a3a6e5808671b112d1878", "2388ed7aee0b6b392778e8f9e98871c06499f476c9e7eae6ca0916f827fe65df", "320a0b5d4900697e125cebb5ff03dee7368f8f087db1c1570b0b62f5a986d759", "90b760ed1d0dcb3ef0f2b6d6195c9d852bcb65eca293578982a8c4b64f51b035", "45313a6745803a7f57ff35f5397fdf117eaec008a76417e6e2ac8a6280f7d830", "e952c18272efa1c3d73d0a5381bcf443c02743fe", "f4d77958a12a0778283d3e679b24b18f82e332c4", "681075027553546c119ec447eb8df84633dcffce", "f8d93c1769e877aae7e7d5c289a467b5ae371c7a", "98ee964edeb5a988c3bba8ea1e57fe0e", "58d4eccc982c9e9b1b98aa62c514e53a", "84ad78b2bab946c3677fdc28ebd8a774", "95dc2289427ed29b8b996d0e3d1b78cb"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
